props.title: Sex and the Single Girl
props.initialSlug: The single life never looked so fun!

sections.content: **Sex and the Single Girl** (1964) represents a pivotal moment in Hollywood's shifting attitudes toward sexuality and gender roles in the mid-1960s. Starring Natalie Wood and Tony Curtis, this romantic comedy deliberately plays with the controversy surrounding Helen Gurley Brown's groundbreaking 1962 advice book of the same name. The film captures the pre-feminist sexual politics of its era, sharing DNA with other sophisticated adult comedies like Pillow Talk (1959) and **That Touch of Mink** (1962). Wood's portrayal of Dr. Helen Brown, a research psychologist specializing in sex, directly challenges the period's professional gender barriers while maintaining the glossy style of high-end Hollywood comedy.

sections.content: The film sits at a fascinating intersection between the dying Production Code era and the emerging sexual revolution. Like **Send Me No Flowers** (1964) and **Sunday in New York** (1963), it uses innuendo and suggestion to push boundaries while maintaining plausible deniability. Director Richard Quine, who previously directed **Bell, Book and Candle** (1958), brings a sophisticated touch that elevates the material beyond mere farce. The film's treatment of female sexuality and career ambition prefigures later works like **The Mary Tyler Moore Show** (1970-1977) and **That Girl** (1966-1971). SUBHEAD: Evolution of the Romantic Comedy

**Sex and the Single Girl** helped bridge the gap between the more innocent romantic comedies of the 1950s and the increasingly frank films of the late 1960s. The chemistry between Wood and Curtis recalls their earlier pairing in **The Great Race** (1965), while the supporting cast including Henry Fonda and Lauren Bacall adds gravitas to the proceedings. The film's exploration of gender roles and sexual politics laid groundwork for later romantic comedies like **Annie Hall** (1977) and **Working Girl** (1988).
